title: conflict over taiwan would be disastrous de facto us ambassador says 2026 09 09
text:
TAIPEI, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Any conflict across the Taiwan Strait would have a bigger impact on the global economy ‌than World War Two, and the upcoming U.S.-China summit is an opportunity to avoid miscalculations, the top U.S. diplomat in Taipei said on Wednesday.
While the U.S., like most countries, has no formal diplomatic relations with Chinese-claimed Taiwan, it is the democratically governed island's most ​important international backer and arms supplier.
Speaking at a defence forum in Taipei, Raymond Greene, director of the ​American Institute in Taiwan, said there was no topic more timely or important than ⁠how to secure peace in the Taiwan Strait.
"Beyond the human toll, any conflict across the Taiwan Strait would have ​a bigger impact on the global economy than the Second World War," he said.
"The United States under the Trump ​administration has made preserving peace in the Indo-Pacific one of its top priorities," Greene added.
That includes "vigorous" diplomacy, especially at the highest levels, he said.
"The upcoming U.S.-China summit is an opportunity to further advance a relationship of strategic stability, on the basis of fairness and reciprocity, ​that can avoid misunderstandings and miscalculations," Greene added.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to travel to the United ​States later this month for a meeting with President Donald Trump.
Greene said that the U.S. was also reinforcing its presence and partnerships ‌in ⁠the Indo-Pacific region to maintain a "favourable regional balance of power".
"Third, and especially relevant to today's discussion, we are supporting Taiwan's work to enhance its ability to defend itself."
Taiwan President Lai Ching-te's administration has made stepped-up defence spending and military modernisation priorities, given the threat level from China.
The government, which rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, has budgeted defence spending for next ​year to exceed T$1 trillion ​for the first time.
Speaking at the same event as Greene, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim said Taiwan has a clear responsibility to strengthen its own defences and make its society better prepared ​to withstand a wide range of security challenges.
"Our purpose, of course, is to preserve ​peace and the ⁠freedom of Taiwan's people to determine their future. Better preparation gives us a basis for pursuing that purpose with steadiness and strength," she added.
China has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, though it says ⁠it would ​prefer a peaceful outcome under a "one country, two systems" model of ​autonomy no major Taiwanese political party supports.
"The reunification of the motherland is an unstoppable historical trend," Chen Binhua, a spokesperson for China's Taiwan Affairs ​Office, told a regular news briefing in Beijing on Wednesday.
